extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, poets and educators interested in Plato's prescriptions for literature and musical/gymnastic education
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and codifies Plato's prescriptions (Republic, Book III) about what stories, styles, musical modes, rhythms, and behaviours are appropriate for the education of guardians in the ideal city. Focuses on censorship of myth/poetry, permitted imitation/narration, musical and gymnastic training, and moral effects of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on undignified depictions of the gods
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets should not depict gods in undignified or excessively humanly humiliating ways (e.g., gods lamenting, rolling in the dirt, exclaiming 'O heavens! ... my heart is sorrowful').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such representations teach youth to fail to respect the divine and to excuse similar weaknesses in themselves; these depictions should be excluded or altered so gods are not misrepresented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbid portraying gods as authors of evil
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets must not teach that the gods are the authors of evil or that heroes (sons of gods) are no better than ordinary men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a poet insists on depicting an impious act associated with a demigod, compel them to either deny the act or deny the divine parentage; do not allow narratives that imply evil comes from gods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid portraying heroes as base or avaricious
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attribute meanness, love of money, or impious insolence to heroic figures (e.g., making Achilles appear greedy or insolent toward Apollo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributing such inconsistent or base motives to celebrated exemplars will corrupt youth's idea of virtue and should be excluded from accepted poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit tales of sexual excess or rape by heroes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not narrate stories where heroes or sons of gods perpetrate sexual crimes (e.g., tales of Theseus or Peirithous committing rape).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such tales are 'impious and dreadful' and will teach lax morals; require poets to remove or recast such episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict tales that portray wicked men as happy
rubrics_metrics.description: Forbid poets from asserting that wicked men are often happy and good men miserable, or that injustice is profitable when undetected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narratives must teach that justice is naturally advantageous to the possessor; stories that glorify injustice will be censored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit rulers limited use of falsehoods for the public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Lying is useless to the gods and harmful to private individuals; however, rulers may be permitted to lie in dealings with enemies or citizens if it serves the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This privilege is restricted to rulers; private citizens who lie to the rulers are to be punished as undermining the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardians must not be given to excessive laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians should not be depicted as overcome by laughter, since fits of excessive laughter almost always produce violent reactions and undermine temperance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry and performance should not encourage frivolity in guardians; representations that depict respected persons laughing immoderately are to be banned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance as key virtue to instill
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperance in youth means obedience to commanders and self-control in sensual pleasures; these are chief elements of temperance to be cultivated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approve and promote language, stories, and musical/rhythmic forms that encourage obedience and self-control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approve language that promotes obedience and respect
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech and verses that encourage obedience to leaders (e.g., Diomede's 'Friend, sit still and obey my word') are to be approved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such expressions foster temperance and proper relation to authority; prefer them over impertinent or mocking addresses to rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbid impertinent or mocking speech toward rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Verses or speech that mock or outrageously insult rulers (e.g., 'O heavy with wine, who hast the eyes of a dog...') are ill spoken and harmful to temperance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although amusing, these forms are likely to corrupt youth's respect for authority and should be excluded from acceptable repertoire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbid celebration of gluttony and drunkenness
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allow songs or verses that extol feasting, overindulgence, or drinking (e.g., lines that glorify tables full of bread and meat and cups of wine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Musical and poetic education should exclude harmonies and lyrics that praise softness, drunkenness, or indolence, because they are unbecoming to guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude depictions that encourage love of money
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject portrayals that recommend taking gifts, assisting for pay, or otherwise glorify avarice (e.g., Phoenix's counsel to Achilles about gifts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heroes should not be represented as mercenary; narratives that normalize taking gifts in exchange for virtue are banned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit imitation of base roles by guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians must not practise or imitate characters unsuited to their role—women quarrelling, persons in sickness, love, labour, slaves performing slave-offices, smiths, oarsmen, boatswains, or other artisan roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation practiced from youth grows into habit and a 'second nature'; restrict guardian imitation to models of courage, temperance, holiness, and freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit imitation of madness, vice, animals, and noises
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians must not be trained to imitate mad or bad men, neighing horses, bellowing bulls, murmuring rivers, thunder, or other pantomimic sounds and behaviours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantomimic imitation (barking, bleating, etc.) fosters vice and inharmonious character and should be excluded from their education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor a narrating (less imitative) style for good men
rubrics_metrics.description: A just and good man, when narrating, will mainly use simple narration with only limited personation of good characters; his style should be largely narrative rather than pantomimic imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narration with restrained imitation better suits the moral temperament expected of guardians; excessive role-assumption is suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject pantomimic/multirole performers for the State
rubrics_metrics.description: Pantomimic performers who imitate everything and assume many roles (tragic, comic, rhapsodist, actor, animal sounds) are not permitted in the ideal State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though popular and admired elsewhere, such multi-role performers are unsuitable because guardians must specialize and avoid corrupting imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow only imitation of virtue (pure imitator of virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Admit into the State only poets and storytellers who imitate virtuous characters; the mixed (pantomimic) style is unsuitable for guardians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the mixed style is charming, the State should favour the 'rougher and severer poet' who imitates virtue only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend censorship to other arts (sculpture, architecture, crafts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Control should extend beyond poets to sculptors, builders, and all creative arts: prohibit exhibition of vice, intemperance, meanness, and indecency in works of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists who cannot conform should be prevented from practising in the State to avoid corrupting citizens' taste and soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music training: ban lamenting and 'relaxed' harmonies
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude harmonies expressive of sorrow and softness — specifically the mixed/tenor Lydian, full-toned/bass Lydian, and the Ionian (and Lydian termed 'relaxed') — because they foster drunkenness and softness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even women of good character should not use these harmonies; music for guardians must avoid strains that encourage intemperance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music training: permit only warlike and temperate harmonies
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserve the Dorian and Phrygian harmonies for the State: one to express the strain of necessity/courage and the other the strain of freedom/temperance (fortune's success with moderation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two harmonies correspond to the 'strain of necessity' and the 'strain of freedom' and are the only harmonies needed for guardians' songs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban panharmonic complexity and certain instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not support makers of multi-cornered lyres, complex scales, or panharmonic instruments; forbid flute-makers and flute-players because the flute is morally worse than stringed instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow only the lyre and harp within the city (a shepherd's pipe in the country), rejecting instrumental complexity that produces morally corrupting music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythms must express courage and harmony; simplicity prized
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose rhythms that are expressions of a courageous and harmonious life; rhythm and harmony should be regulated by the words (and the soul's temper), not the other way around.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid multiplicity of metres and complex metrical systems; consult expert (Damon) to assign rhythms that correspond to virtues and vices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty of style depends on simplicity of soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty of style, harmony, grace, and good rhythm depend on true simplicity — the simplicity of a rightly ordered mind and character, not foolish simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Musical and literary education should aim to cultivate this inner simplicity so that perception and taste form around virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical training as the most potent formative instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: Musical training (rhythm and harmony) most deeply enters the soul, imparting grace and making the rightly educated person graceful; it enables perception of omissions or faults in art and nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because music fastens on the 'inward places of the soul,' it should be central to early education to instill taste and virtue before reason is fully developed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gymnastic training begins early and continues through life
rubrics_metrics.description: After musical education, gymnastics is next in order: training should begin in early years, be careful, and continue through life; the good soul improves the body rather than the reverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gymnastics complements musical training to produce citizens whose bodies reflect their cultivated souls; both are essential parts of guardians' education.
